finding.headline: You can count on $42,000 a year: $39,100 for basics and $2,900 for the rest.
details: Your basics cost about $39,100 a year.
Your spending goal of $51,000 a year lasts in 28 of 100 scenarios.

assumptions: All figures are in today's dollars: what money buys now, not the larger sums prices will reach.

Savings grow on average 5.0% a year above inflation in stocks and 1.8% in bonds, with good and bad years. The plan tests many possible market paths. These are planning figures, not a forecast. They are fixed, so every plan is tested on the same markets; to see a bad stretch, try a What If such as markets fall 30%.

Social Security uses the figure you gave, read as the benefit at 67. Your answers show $23,200 a year from 67. This plan starts it at 70 for you and 67 for your partner, which pays about $26,900 a year.
A partner with little pay of their own gets half of the other's benefit at 67, less if started sooner.
After the first death (at the shorter life expectancy), Social Security falls to the larger of your two benefits, about $19,200 a year, and spending falls to 75% of what the two of you spend.

Tax uses the 2027 federal brackets, the standard deduction and your state's rates. In retirement the plan counts 85% of Social Security as taxable, the most the law allows, so the tax may be a little high.
The plan runs to age 96. There is about a 1 in 4 chance that one of you will live that long (US life table, SOA 2024). People with more money tend to live longer than that table says.
